stem_html:
Linguist Mira Osei describes the grammar of a creole as ______ rather than borrowed. The features that distinguish it appear in no one of the languages that met at its birth, and the children who first spoke it had no model to copy them from.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "invented"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "inherited", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "simplified", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "contested", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Rather than” sets the polarity. One choice simply repeats the term being ruled out.
  • The stereotype about creoles. “Simplified” is the word most readers associate with them, and the passage never raises complexity.
  • Both halves of the evidence are negative — no source language, no model — which is what forces a positive word into the blank.

Why A is right The second sentence rules out every source: the features appear in no one of the languages that met at its birth, and the children who first spoke it had no model to copy them from. Something that comes from no source was made.

Why B is wrong Inherited is a synonym for the word the sentence contrasts the blank with. A grammar that was inherited would be borrowed, which is the alternative Osei rejects.

Why C is wrong Simplified says something about the grammar's complexity relative to its sources, and the sentence is about origin instead. It is also a claim the evidence does not touch.

Why D is wrong Contested would mean people argue about the grammar. Nothing in the passage reports a dispute; the second sentence is a description of where the features came from.

stem_html:
The court's ruling was widely reported as a defeat for the agency, but its practical effect was ______: the agency lost the power it had exercised only twice in forty years and kept every authority it uses week to week.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "negligible"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "devastating", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "ambiguous", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "delayed", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “But” is the instruction. The blank must contradict “a defeat.”
  • Two facts after the colon, one lost and one kept, and both point the same way.
  • Uncertainty is not smallness. A precisely described small effect is not an ambiguous one.

Why A is right The colon spells out what was actually lost: a power exercised only twice in forty years, with every everyday authority intact. That is a change that barely registers in practice.

Why B is wrong Devastating repeats the reported reading rather than the practical one. The sentence turns on “but,” so the blank has to disagree with what was widely reported.

Why C is wrong Ambiguous would mean the effect is hard to determine. The clause after the colon is unusually precise about what was lost and what was kept.

Why D is wrong Delayed concerns timing, and the sentence says nothing about when the effect arrives. It contrasts the size of the effect with the size of the headline.

stem_html:
Archivists once treated the marginalia in library copies as ______, scrubbing pencil from the margins as a matter of course. The same annotations are now catalogued and photographed, because a note in a 1920s hand records something the printed page cannot: what a reader of that decade found worth arguing with.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "damage"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "evidence", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "decoration", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "commentary", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two eras in one text. The blank belongs to the earlier one, and the most quotable sentence describes the later one.
  • A neutral term where a judgement is needed. The word has to explain the scrubbing.
  • “Now” in the second sentence is the marker that separates the two attitudes.

Why A is right The clause after the blank is the definition: they scrubbed pencil from the margins as a matter of course. Something routinely removed from a book was being treated as harm done to it.

Why B is wrong Evidence is what archivists treat the marginalia as now, which the second sentence describes. The first sentence needs the earlier and opposite attitude.

Why C is wrong Decoration would explain neither the scrubbing nor the reversal. A decorative marking is not obviously worth destroying and not obviously worth photographing.

Why D is wrong Commentary is an accurate description of what marginalia are, and it gives no reason to erase them. The blank has to carry the old evaluation, not a neutral label.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2023 article about coral reefs.

Reef managers rank sites for protection by the fraction of live coral they carry, and the highest-scoring sites are the ones that receive patrols and moorings. Akintola's ten-year record from the Coral Triangle complicates that ranking. The sites that recovered fastest after the 2016 bleaching were not the ones with the most live coral beforehand but the ones with the widest range of coral growth forms, and several of those had scored poorly enough to be left off the protection list. Akintola does not argue that cover should be abandoned as a criterion; she argues that it is a poor proxy for what managers actually want, which is a reef that comes back.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It reports evidence that a widely used ranking criterion measures something other than the outcome managers care about."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It argues that reef protection programmes should be discontinued because their criteria are flawed.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It describes the 2016 bleaching event and its effects on the Coral Triangle.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It proposes a new method for measuring the range of coral growth forms at a site.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The sentence written to stop the overreach. The passage denies the strongest reading of itself, and one choice takes it anyway.
  • Background promoted to subject. The bleaching is a date, not a topic.
  • A finding read as a proposal. Identifying the better predictor is not offering a way to measure it.

Why A is right The passage names the criterion, shows it does not predict recovery, and says so explicitly: she argues that it is a poor proxy for what managers actually want, which is a reef that comes back.

Why B is wrong The last sentence forecloses this: Akintola does not argue that cover should be abandoned as a criterion. Discontinuing the programmes is a further step still.

Why C is wrong The bleaching is the event her record is measured against, not the subject. The passage spends its length on the ranking, not on the bleaching.

Why D is wrong Growth-form range is the variable that turned out to predict recovery. No method for measuring it is proposed or described.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from Anton Chekhov's 1899 story “The Lady with the Dog.”

He had two lives: one open, seen and known by all who cared to know, full of relative truth and of relative falsehood, exactly like the lives of his friends and acquaintances; and another life running its course in secret. And through some strange, perhaps accidental, conjunction of circumstances, everything that was essential, of interest and of value to him, everything in which he was sincere and did not deceive himself, everything that made the kernel of his life, was hidden from other people.

Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It specifies which of the two lives introduced in the first sentence holds what matters to him."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It explains why the character has kept his second life secret from his friends.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It contrasts the character's sincerity with the deception practised by his acquaintances.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It suggests that the character's open life is entirely false.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A cause named without being given. “Some strange conjunction of circumstances” is a refusal to explain.
  • “Relative” twice. The open life is qualified in both directions, so it cannot be summarised as false.
  • Function against content. Three choices report something in the sentence; one says what the sentence does.

Why A is right The first sentence names two lives and describes only the open one. The second loads the hidden one with everything that made the kernel of his life, which is where the passage puts its weight.

Why B is wrong No reason for the secrecy is given. The narration reports the division and calls the cause a strange, perhaps accidental, conjunction of circumstances, which explains nothing.

Why C is wrong The acquaintances appear in the first sentence, and they are said to live exactly as he does. The second sentence draws no contrast with them.

Why D is wrong The open life is called full of relative truth and of relative falsehood, which is a mixture rather than a lie. “Entirely false” hardens a careful phrase.

stem_html:
Text 1

Ravens and crows solve puzzles that defeat most mammals, and the usual explanation is social: species that live in large, shifting groups need to track who owes what to whom, and that bookkeeping selects for general intelligence.

Text 2

Mendes tested nineteen corvid species on the same set of puzzles. Group size predicted nothing. What predicted performance was the breadth of the species' diet: the birds that extracted food from many kinds of hiding place solved the puzzles fastest, whether they lived in flocks of two hundred or in pairs.

Based on the texts, how would Mendes (Text 2) most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "By pointing out that the variable it names does not predict performance, while a different variable does."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "By arguing that corvids are less intelligent than Text 1 assumes.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "By agreeing with it and adding diet breadth as a second social factor.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "By noting that large groups are found only in species with broad diets.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Adding rather than replacing. One choice keeps the social account and bolts the new finding onto it.
  • “Whether they lived in flocks of two hundred or in pairs” is the clause that breaks the link between the two variables.
  • Doubting the ability instead of the explanation.

Why A is right Mendes tested the social explanation directly and it failed: group size predicted nothing, while the breadth of the species' diet did predict performance. That is a rejection plus a replacement.

Why B is wrong Her birds solved the puzzles, some of them fastest. Nothing in Text 2 lowers the estimate of corvid intelligence; it relocates the cause.

Why C is wrong Diet breadth is a foraging variable, not a social one, and she does not agree with Text 1 — the social variable came out flat.

Why D is wrong Text 2 says the opposite: the fastest solvers included birds living in pairs, so broad diets are found across group sizes.

stem_html:
Hydrologist Sanne Bakker proposed that the reason a restored floodplain stores less water than an undisturbed one is the compaction left by farm machinery, not the age of the restoration. She predicted that a restored site's storage should track how heavily it was worked before restoration rather than how long ago it was restored.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Bakker's proposal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Among sites restored in the same year, those that had carried the heaviest machinery stored the least water; among sites with the same machinery history, storage did not vary with year of restoration."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Sites restored more than twenty years ago stored more water than sites restored within the last five years.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Undisturbed floodplains stored more water than restored floodplains of every age.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Soil samples from restored sites had a higher bulk density than samples from undisturbed sites.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two variables, one comparison each. Only a finding that holds one constant can separate them.
  • The rival pattern offered as support. One choice is the age explanation stated as a result.
  • Confirming the phenomenon rather than the cause.

Why A is right She predicted that a restored site's storage should track how heavily it was worked before restoration rather than how long ago it was restored. The prediction pits two variables against each other, so the evidence has to hold each one fixed in turn. Machinery matters when age is held constant, and age does not matter when machinery is held constant.

Why B is wrong This is the pattern Bakker's proposal predicts will not appear. Storage rising with time since restoration is the age explanation she is arguing against.

Why C is wrong That restored sites underperform is the fact being explained and is agreed by both accounts. It cannot distinguish them.

Why D is wrong Higher bulk density is compaction, which is consistent with Bakker, but it says nothing about water storage and nothing about age. It supplies half of one side of the comparison.

stem_html:
A team studying an eighteenth-century shipwreck claims the vessel was carrying cargo rather than ballast when it sank, on the grounds that a ship in ballast would show stone distributed evenly along the keel while a laden ship would show it concentrated where the cargo was not.

Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the team's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The stone recovered from the wreck lies in two dense clusters at the bow and stern, with almost none amidships."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The stone recovered from the wreck is of a type quarried two hundred kilometres from the ship's home port.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The total mass of stone recovered is consistent with the mass a ship of this size would carry in ballast.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Timbers from the wreck show the ship was riding low in the water when it sank.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The stated test is the whole question. The team names distribution, and three choices measure something else.
  • Mass where the argument is about arrangement.
  • A fact compatible with both hypotheses supports neither.

Why A is right The team's test is about distribution: a ship in ballast would show stone distributed evenly along the keel, and a laden one would show it concentrated where the cargo was not. Two dense clusters with a gap amidships is exactly the concentrated pattern.

Why B is wrong Where the stone was quarried bears on trade routes, not on how the stone sat in the hull. The claim is decided by arrangement.

Why C is wrong A ballast-sized mass points the other way. It is the quantity a ship in ballast would carry, which is the alternative the team rejects.

Why D is wrong Riding low means heavily loaded, which is consistent with cargo and equally consistent with a full load of ballast. It does not separate the two.

stem_html:
Students in four sections of the same course were given the same final exam. Sections 1 and 2 had used spaced practice; sections 3 and 4 had used massed practice. The instructor concluded that spaced practice raised scores and that the size of the gain did not depend on how many hours a section had studied.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the instructor's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The two spaced sections scored about 12 points above the two massed sections, and within each pair the section that studied more did not score higher."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Section 1 scored higher than section 4, and section 1 studied fewer hours than section 4.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The section with the most study hours scored higher than the section with the fewest.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "All four sections scored above 70.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Comparing across conditions when the point is within them. Study hours can only be tested by holding practice type fixed.
  • A single pair of bars. The conclusion is about all four.
  • A true statement about the graph that tests nothing.

Why A is right The instructor concluded that spaced practice raised scores and that the size of the gain did not depend on how many hours a section had studied. Both halves of the conclusion appear: the 12-point gap between the spaced pair and the massed pair is the gain, and within each pair the section with more hours scored the same or slightly lower, which is the independence from study time.

Why B is wrong One comparison across the two conditions confounds practice type with study hours, so it cannot show that hours are irrelevant. It uses two of the four bars and leaves the pattern untested.

Why C is wrong Section 4 studied 33 hours and section 3 studied 21, and section 4 scored 72 against section 3's 71 — but the highest scorer, section 1, studied 22. As stated the claim also runs against the instructor's second point.

Why D is wrong Every section clearing 70 is a true reading with no bearing on either half of the conclusion.

stem_html: In her sequence Field Notes, the poet Adaeze Nwosu presents the act of naming a plant as something that puts distance between the speaker and what she is looking at. Which quotation from a fictional poem would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "“I said bindweed, and the white bell went / from a thing I was watching to a thing I knew.”"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "“I could not name the white bell on the fence, / and stood there until the light had gone.”", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "“Bindweed, convolvulus, hedge-bell — the names / are three and the flower is one.”", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "“My grandmother knew the names of all of them, / and taught me none, and I have had to guess.”", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The claim is about an act and its effect. Two choices supply an act with no effect, or an effect with no act.
  • The absence of naming is not naming.
  • Many names for one thing is a claim about language, not about attention.

Why A is right Nwosu presents the act of naming a plant as something that puts distance between the speaker and what she is looking at, and here the naming is the hinge of the line and the effect is a move away: the flower goes from a thing I was watching to a thing I knew. Attention is exchanged for classification, which is the distance the claim describes.

Why B is wrong Here the speaker cannot name the plant and stays with it, which is the situation the claim's logic implies but not the act the claim is about. Nothing is named.

Why C is wrong This is about the multiplicity of names, a different observation. The flower is not moved away by any of them; it is simply one thing with three labels.

Why D is wrong This is about inheritance and its absence. Naming happens off the page, in the grandmother's generation, and no effect on the speaker's looking is shown.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2022 article about the Antikythera mechanism.

The device's gearing has been reconstructed from fragments many times, and each reconstruction has been judged by whether its gear ratios reproduce known astronomical cycles. Ampatzis points out that this test is weaker than it looks: with enough gears, many ratios can be made to approximate a given cycle, so a reconstruction that matches is not thereby shown to be the original. His own model is offered on a different basis — every gear in it corresponds to a surviving fragment, and no gear has been added to make the arithmetic work.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "A reconstruction should be judged by its fit to the surviving physical evidence rather than by its ability to reproduce astronomical cycles."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The Antikythera mechanism's gear ratios reproduce several known astronomical cycles.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Ampatzis's model is the first reconstruction to reproduce the device's astronomical cycles accurately.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Earlier reconstructions of the mechanism contained arithmetic errors.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • An argument about method, read as an argument about results.
  • “Not thereby shown” is a claim about inference, not a claim that the earlier models are wrong.
  • The dash introduces the replacement criterion, which is where the main idea lives.

Why A is right The passage attacks a criterion and offers another. The old test cannot distinguish models because many ratios can be made to approximate a given cycle; the new one is that every gear in it corresponds to a surviving fragment.

Why B is wrong This is the assumption behind the old test, mentioned as background. It is not in dispute and it is not the point.

Why C is wrong Ampatzis explicitly declines to rest on cycle reproduction. Claiming he does it best inverts his argument.

Why D is wrong No arithmetic error is alleged. The complaint is that matching arithmetic is too easy, which is the opposite of a claim that earlier models got it wrong.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2020 article about the Great Migration.

Between 1916 and 1970 some six million Black Americans left the rural South. Histories of the movement have usually explained it through conditions in the places people left. Reading the letters that migrants sent home, Whitfield finds the decisive information often ran the other way: a cousin in Chicago wrote what the packing houses paid that month, and a family moved. The letters, she argues, were an employment service that the census cannot see.

According to the text, what does Whitfield's reading of the letters indicate about the migration?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Information sent back from destination cities influenced when and where families moved."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Conditions in the rural South were not severe enough to cause the migration.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Most migrants moved to Chicago rather than to other northern cities.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Census records are the most reliable source for studying the migration.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Adding a cause is not denying another. The strongest-sounding choice removes the reason everybody already knows.
  • The one named city is an illustration.
  • The last clause is about what the census misses, and one choice reverses it.

Why A is right The letters carried news northward to southward: a cousin in Chicago wrote what the packing houses paid that month, and a family moved. Whitfield calls that an employment service, which is information driving the decision.

Why B is wrong Whitfield adds a factor rather than removing one. Saying the letters mattered does not say conditions in the South did not.

Why C is wrong Chicago is the example in the one sentence that gives a city. No claim about the distribution of destinations is made.

Why D is wrong The passage says the letters are an employment service that the census cannot see, which is a limit on the census, not an endorsement of it.

stem_html:
A pesticide is applied to a field every spring, and the target insect has become resistant to it. Resistance is known to carry a cost: in the absence of the pesticide, resistant individuals reproduce more slowly than susceptible ones. On one farm the pesticide has been used every year for a decade and resistance is near total; on a neighbouring farm the same pesticide is used in alternate years only, and resistance there has stayed below a fifth of the population. Since the two populations interbreed freely and face the same weather, it can be concluded that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the pesticide-free years allow the reproductive cost of resistance to reduce its frequency in the population."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "the insects on the second farm have not yet been exposed to the pesticide long enough to develop resistance.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "resistance carries no reproductive cost in this species.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "alternating the pesticide would eliminate resistance entirely if continued long enough.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The premise names the mechanism. The conclusion has to use it rather than deny it.
  • “Interbreed freely” closes the exposure explanation. The two populations share genes.
  • A stable fraction is not a falling one, so extrapolating to zero goes past the evidence.

Why A is right The two farms differ in one respect, the years without pesticide, and the premise supplies the mechanism: in the absence of the pesticide, resistant individuals reproduce more slowly. The gap years let that cost act.

Why B is wrong Both farms have had the pesticide for the same decade, and the populations interbreed freely, so the second farm's insects have had the same exposure and the same genes available.

Why C is wrong The cost is given as known in the second sentence, and it is the fact that makes the pattern explicable. Denying it removes the only available explanation.

Why D is wrong Nothing here supports elimination. Resistance has stayed below a fifth rather than falling toward zero, and the passage gives no trend over time.

stem_html:
A city introduced a fee on single-use bags at supermarkets. Sales of small plastic bin liners at the same supermarkets rose by 78 percent in the following year, and total plastic tonnage collected from household waste fell by only 3 percent, far less than the drop in single-use bags alone would predict. Since household numbers and waste collection routes were unchanged, it can be concluded that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "many households had been reusing single-use bags for a purpose they now buy bin liners for."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "the fee failed to reduce the number of single-use bags taken from supermarkets.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "households in the city produce more waste than they did before the fee.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "fees on single-use items never reduce plastic consumption.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two numbers pointing different ways. A big behavioural change and a small tonnage change is the shape of a substitution.
  • Reading the comparison backwards. The clause about what the bag drop “would predict” presupposes the drop happened.
  • One case, one year.

Why A is right Bin liner sales rose sharply while total tonnage barely moved, which is one plastic substituting for another. That happens only if the bags had been doing the liners' job.

Why B is wrong The passage assumes the drop in single-use bags was large — it says the tonnage fell far less than the drop in single-use bags alone would predict. The fee worked on bags; the tonnage is the puzzle.

Why C is wrong Total tonnage fell, if only slightly. Nothing indicates more waste, and household numbers were unchanged.

Why D is wrong One city and one year cannot support a claim about fees in general, and even here the reduction was real, if small.

stem_html:
The observatory sits at 4,200 metres, where the air holds little water vapour ______ is the property that matters most for infrared astronomy.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", which"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; which", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "which", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": which", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A relative clause is never independent, whatever its length.
  • Essential against nonessential. The comma is what tells the reader the clause refers to the whole preceding statement.
  • Two strong marks that both need a full clause on the right.

Why A is right The clause beginning “which” is a nonessential relative clause commenting on the whole idea before it, and such a clause is set off with a comma.

Why B is wrong A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and a relative clause introduced by “which” is dependent.

Why C is wrong Without the comma the clause reads as essential and attaches to “water vapour,” which reverses the meaning: it is the scarcity of vapour, not the vapour, that matters.

Why D is wrong A colon introduces an explanation or a list and cannot be followed by a relative pronoun continuing the same sentence.

stem_html:
Manuscript illuminators ground their own pigments, and the most expensive of them, ultramarine, came from a single valley in what is now Afghanistan ______ the blue in a European psalter had travelled five thousand kilometres before it touched the page.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "; ultimately"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", ultimately", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "ultimately", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "and ultimately", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • An adverb is not a conjunction. “Ultimately,” “however” and “therefore” all create splices when a comma is the only mark.
  • The first clause is long and already contains commas, which makes one more feel harmless.
  • “And” without its comma.

Why A is right Two independent clauses meet with only an adverb between them, and “ultimately” is not a conjunction. A semicolon is what joins them.

Why B is wrong A comma plus an adverb is still a comma between two independent clauses, which is a splice. Conjunctive adverbs do not do the work of conjunctions.

Why C is wrong With no punctuation the clauses fuse, and the adverb is left ambiguously attached to either of them.

Why D is wrong “And” could join the clauses, but it needs a comma in front of it when it joins two independent clauses of this length, and none is offered.

stem_html:
Only three of the bridge's original cables ______ replaced in the 1978 refit, remain in service today.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", all of which were"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "all of which were", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "; all of which were", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "all of them were", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The closing comma is already on the page. The question is what opens the pair.
  • “Which” against “them.” One keeps the clause dependent and one does not.
  • Subject and verb are far apart, which makes an intrusive strong mark feel acceptable.

Why A is right The nonessential clause is closed by the comma already printed before “remain,” so it must be opened by a comma too. “All of which” keeps the clause relative and therefore attachable.

Why B is wrong Without the opening comma the interruption has only one boundary, and the sentence appears to say the cables were replaced and remain in service, which is not what the punctuation after it allows.

Why C is wrong A semicolon cannot open a nonessential clause, and it would separate the subject from its verb.

Why D is wrong “All of them were” is an independent clause, so inserting it here leaves two clauses joined by commas alone.

stem_html:
The problem with the standard account is not that it lacks evidence ______ has too much, and no way to decide which of its many supporting cases is load-bearing.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

Traps in this question

  • “Not that ... it has” is a correction structure, and it still needs a mark strong enough for two clauses.
  • A conjunction that fixes the grammar and breaks the meaning.
  • The second clause has its own subject and verb, which is the only test that matters.

Why A is right Both sides are independent clauses joined without a conjunction, so a semicolon is required. The contrast between “not that it lacks” and “it has too much” does not license a weaker mark.

Why B is wrong A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice however sharp the contrast is.

Why C is wrong With no mark at all the sentence fuses and the reader briefly attaches “it” to “evidence.”

Why D is wrong “And” is grammatical but wrong in sense: the second clause corrects the first rather than adding to it, and the sentence is built on that opposition.

The archive's collection of glass negatives, together with the ledgers that record who commissioned each portrait, ______ the only surviving account of the studio's clientele.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "constitutes"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "constitute", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "have constituted", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "are", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Together with” is not “and.” The same is true of “as well as” and “in addition to.”
  • Two plural nouns between subject and verb.
  • The singular verb sounds wrong aloud, which is exactly why the rule has to be applied rather than heard.

Why A is right The subject is “collection,” which is singular. “Together with” introduces an accompanying phrase and does not create a compound subject.

Why B is wrong Plural agreement follows “negatives” or “ledgers,” both of which sit inside modifiers rather than in the subject slot.

Why C is wrong This is plural for the same reason and adds a present perfect the sentence has no use for.

Why D is wrong “Are” is plural, and it also flattens the sentence: the predicate names what the collection constitutes, which the verb should carry.

Why D is wrong “There” is an expletive subject with no content for the modifier to attach to.

By the time the last of the wolves was removed from the park in 1926, the elk herd ______ to more than four times the size it had been at the turn of the century.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "had grown"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "has grown", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "grows", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "is growing", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “By the time” is the sequence marker.
  • “It had been” later in the sentence shows the sentence is already working in the past perfect.
  • Every wrong choice is present tense, and each of them reads acceptably on its own.

Why A is right “By the time” establishes one past event, the removal in 1926, and requires the earlier one, the herd's growth, in the past perfect.

Why B is wrong The present perfect links a past event to the present, and this sentence closes in 1926.

Why C is wrong Simple present puts a completed historical change into the reader's own time.

Why D is wrong The present progressive describes something happening now, which no part of this sentence is.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Three candidate antecedents in one sentence.
  • The possessive that is not one. “It's” never means “belonging to it.”
  • A grammatical pronoun with an unclear referent is still an error on this test.

Why A is right Two editions are in play, so a pronoun cannot say which one the commas belong to. Naming the edition is what makes the sentence say something.

Why B is wrong “Its” could point to either edition or to the poem, and the sentence supplies nothing to choose among them.

Why C is wrong “Their” is plural and would refer to both editions or to the scholars, neither of which is the intended owner of the commas.

Why D is wrong “It's” is the contraction of “it is” and cannot show possession at all.

stem_html:
The standard treatment for the infection is a two-week course of antibiotics, and shortening it is generally discouraged. ______ a trial of 1,100 patients found that a five-day course cleared the infection in the same proportion of cases and produced fewer relapses at six months.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Even so,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "As a result,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "In other words,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Likewise,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The first sentence reports a norm, not the writer's view, and the second supplies evidence against it.
  • Consequence where there is contradiction.
  • Two choices assert agreement between sentences that conflict.

Why A is right The trial result runs against the advice just given, so the transition has to mark opposition. “Even so” acknowledges the standard and then reports the finding that cuts against it.

Why B is wrong “As a result” would make the trial a consequence of the discouragement, which reverses cause and evidence.

Why C is wrong “In other words” restates. The second sentence introduces new data, not a paraphrase.

Why D is wrong “Likewise” needs agreement between the sentences, and they disagree.

stem_html:
Peregrine falcons were nearly extirpated from the eastern United States by the 1960s. Captive-bred birds were released from towers and bridges beginning in 1974. ______ the eastern population now exceeds its estimated pre-decline size.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Today,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "However,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "For example,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "By contrast,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A three-step chronology. The transition marks time, not opposition.
  • The first sentence is the one the last contrasts with, and the transition sits next to the second.
  • Result against example.

Why A is right The three sentences form a chronology: near loss, intervention, present state. A time marker is what carries the reader to the last stage.

Why B is wrong “However” announces a reversal of the previous sentence, but the recovery is the intended outcome of the releases rather than a surprise against them.

Why C is wrong The current population size is the result of the releases, not an instance of them.

Why D is wrong “By contrast” sets the third sentence against the second, when the second is what produced the third.
